nameStory: The West Virginia White got its name from where it was first scientifically described, though it's found far beyond West Virginia's borders. This delicate butterfly ranges throughout the Appalachian Mountains and Great Lakes region, making New England part of its natural home territory.
description: The West Virginia White is a small, delicate butterfly with translucent white wings that seem to glow in dappled forest light. Unlike many white butterflies, it typically lacks any yellowish tinge, appearing as a pure, clean white that almost looks like tissue paper floating through the woods. These ethereal butterflies are about the size of a quarter when their wings are spread, and their semi-transparent wings give them an almost ghostly appearance as they flutter through shaded woodland areas.

idTips.label: Semi-transparent wings
idTips.description: Wings have a delicate, tissue-paper quality that lets light shine through, creating an almost ghostly appearance unlike the solid white of other butterflies

idTips.label: Pure white coloration
idTips.description: Lacks the yellowish or cream tinge common in other white butterflies, appearing as a clean, bright white that stands out in shadowy forests

idTips.label: Hindwing vein patterns
idTips.description: Underside of hindwings shows subtle tawny, gray, or pale brown coloring along the veins, visible when wings are closed

idTips.label: Forest habitat preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively in moist deciduous woodlands, never in open fields or gardens where other white butterflies are common

idTips.label: Early spring timing
idTips.description: Active only during a brief window in April or May, often flying when few other butterflies are on the wing

habitat: West Virginia Whites inhabit moist deciduous forests, particularly those with rich, humusy soil that supports their host plants in the mustard family. Look for them in mature woodlands with a mix of hardwood trees like maples, oaks, and birches, especially in areas with spring wildflowers. They prefer shaded forest floors and clearings within the woods rather than forest edges or open areas.

seasonality.spring: Active adults fly for just one month in April or May, making this your only chance to see them. They emerge early to coincide with their host plants' growing season and can be seen nectaring on spring wildflowers.
seasonality.summer: No adult butterflies are present - the species exists only as eggs, caterpillars, or pupae developing on woodland mustard plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults are completely absent, with the next generation developing through larval stages on host plants in preparation for winter.
seasonality.winter: The species overwinters in pupal form, hidden away in the leaf litter and soil of the forest floor until spring emergence.

funFact: West Virginia Whites are disappearing from parts of their range because they mistake the invasive garlic mustard plant for their native host plants, laying eggs on it only to have their caterpillars starve since they can't actually digest this foreign invader.
confusionNotes: Often confused with the more common Small White (cabbage white), but remember: if you see a white butterfly in your garden or open fields, it's NOT a West Virginia White - these woodland specialists stick to shady forests and have that distinctive tissue-paper transparency that garden whites lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting a limited range, the West Virginia White is actually found throughout much of eastern North America. However, it's becoming increasingly rare due to forest fragmentation and the spread of invasive garlic mustard, making each sighting particularly special for nature observers.
compareHints: West Virginia Whites differ from their close relatives, the Small White and Mustard White, by their exclusive forest habitat and translucent wing quality. While Small Whites are common garden visitors with more solid white wings, and Mustard Whites can be found in various open habitats, West Virginia Whites never venture far from their woodland homes and maintain that characteristic see-through appearance that makes them unmistakable in their forest setting.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Small White differs from its native relatives, the Mustard White and West Virginia White, by having more opaque, bright white wings and distinct black spots rather than the translucent, checkered appearance of the native species.
Unlike the Small White (an introduced species that's more tolerant of disturbed areas), the mustard white sticks to wilder habitats and shows distinct seasonal forms.
